script.opening_words:
Cole is sitting on a pile of cash
waiting. He's not panicking, not
chasing. He's disciplined. He's going to
wait for the next big crash and when
everyone else is losing their minds,
he's going to back up the truck and buy.
Carol on the other hand throws $300 into
an index fund on the first of every
month and genuinely does not care what
the market is doing. All time high, she
buys. Blood in the streets, she buys.
She might be the laziest investor
script.ending_words:
ensible, and the line between
smart rebalancing and Cole fooling
himself is thinner and more interesting
than you'd expect, but that's a whole
different conversation, and the math
behind it might surprise you even more
than what you just saw. For now, the
next time someone tells you they're
waiting for a better entry point, that
they're keeping their cash ready for the
next big crash, just ask them one
question. How long are you willing to
wait? Because the market doesn't owe you
a crash, and while you're waiting for
the perfect moment, the only thing
compounding is the cost of waiting for
it.
script.analysis: All 17,757 stored characters read in three contiguous ranges with canonical hash match. Paired characters Cole (cash, waits for crash) versus Carol ($300/month automatic index fund). Hook teases that even an all-knowing dip buyer loses. Body: 2009-2020 bull market, record-high frequency and permanent floors, positive-year frequency, Schwab 20-year timing study (perfect/DCA/worst/cash), 1928 $100 stocks versus cash, Maggiulli omniscient buy-the-dip versus DCA across 40-year windows and the two-month-miss result, single March 2009 purchase share, mid-video "school community" CTA, correction/bear frequency, honest counter-section (2009 and 2020 bottom returns, average 12-month post-bear return ~47%, rebalancing/lump-sum legitimate use), Dalbar behavior gap and outflows, Carol automation payoff, close posing the "dry powder plus DCA" follow-up. Research-dense with named sources and a fair counterargument; best credibility among this batch. Main framing issue: Schwab's cash investor never invested at all, so it is not identical to Cole buying after crashes. No subscribe CTA at start. ASR not audio-verified.

claim_audit: 0:7000 Schwab study confirmed (search excerpt): perfect timing $186,007, monthly DCA $166,591, worst timing $151,343, cash $47,357 over 20 years at $2,000/year; script figures $186K/$166K/$47K and "worst still tripled cash" (3.2x) correct. Perfect beat DCA by ~$19.4K (~$1,000/year), consistent. But Schwab's cash investor never bought stocks, so applying it to Cole (who buys after crashes) overstates Cole's shortfall; Schwab inputs are $2,000/year, not Carol's $300/month. 2009-2020 bull ~11 years and roughly 400% total return consistent with widely cited figures. Record highs on ~7% of days since 1950 and "almost a third never revisited" not verified here. Positive ~3 of 4 years consistent with long-run S&P history.

7000:14000 $100 in 1928 to over $1M in stocks versus ~$2,500 in cash consistent with NYU Stern (Damodaran) historical-return tables in nominal terms, not verified here; inflation not discussed. Maggiulli "Even God Couldn't Beat Dollar-Cost Averaging": DCA beat omniscient buy-the-dip in >70% of 40-year periods since 1920 and missing the bottom by two months loses ~97% of the time - consistent with the published analysis as commonly cited; not re-accessed here. Corrections ~annual, bear markets ~every 3.5 years and ~1 in 4 corrections becoming bears consistent with common historical summaries; March 2009 10-year ~17.5%/year and March 2020 4-year ~25%/year approximately consistent with S&P total-return history; 13-bear average 12-month post-bottom ~47% unverified.

14000:17757 Dalbar QAIB figures (market ~25% vs average equity investor ~16.5%, outflows each quarter, 15 straight years of underperformance) consistent with Dalbar's 2025 report as publicized; Dalbar methodology has known critiques (flow-based estimates), not mentioned. Carol's 40-year portfolio outcome stated qualitatively without numbers. DCA buying more shares when prices fall is correct mechanics.
